findings.title: Valid JSON with an unexpected shape can escape update handling
findings.description: JsonElement.TryGetProperty throws InvalidOperationException when invoked on a non-object value. A sidecar whose root is an array or whose `unit` value is not an object therefore escapes the current catch filter. During initial enumeration this aborts construction; from a watcher callback it becomes an unhandled event-handler exception instead of merely leaving the sidecar unindexed.
findings.recommendation: Check `ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Object` before each property lookup and treat shape mismatches as invalid metadata. As a defensive boundary, ensure watcher callbacks cannot propagate parsing or validation exceptions.

findings.title: Invalid replacements leave previously indexed metadata active
findings.description: Every validation failure and every caught read or parse failure returns without changing `documents`. If an existing valid sidecar is overwritten with permanently malformed or invalid content, its old payload remains returned by `Read`; `Find` also returns it because the file still exists. This contradicts the comment that malformed sidecars stay unindexed.
findings.recommendation: Distinguish transient read failures from successfully read but invalid content. Remove the existing entry when validation conclusively fails, and use a bounded retry or debounce strategy for transient filesystem races so a failed notification cannot leave stale data indefinitely.

findings.title: Files can be missed between the initial scan and watcher activation
findings.description: The repository is fully enumerated before the FileSystemWatcher is constructed and enabled. A qualifying file created after enumeration passes its directory but before events are enabled is neither indexed by the scan nor reported by the watcher, and can remain absent until another filesystem change occurs.
findings.recommendation: Establish the watcher before scanning and reconcile with a second scan after event capture begins, or otherwise buffer events and perform an atomic scan-and-subscribe sequence with deduplication.

findings.title: Concurrent first access can create undisposed repository indexes
findings.description: ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd may invoke its value factory more than once for the same key. Each factory invocation constructs and enables a FileSystemWatcher, but only one RepositoryIndex is stored; discarded instances are never disposed and can continue receiving events until collected.
findings.recommendation: Store `Lazy<RepositoryIndex>` values with execution-and-publication semantics, or serialize repository creation and explicitly dispose any candidate that loses the insertion race.

findings.title: Watcher event loss is not detected or reconciled
findings.description: FileSystemWatcher can report errors, including internal buffer overflow, after which one or more changes may have been lost. No `Error` handler or periodic reconciliation exists, so the in-memory index can silently diverge from disk for the remainder of its lifetime.
findings.recommendation: Handle the watcher's `Error` event and rebuild or reconcile the repository index. Keep rebuilding synchronized with normal event processing, and consider exposing diagnostics when recovery fails.

findings.title: Filesystem monitoring behavior cannot be tested deterministically
findings.description: RepositoryIndex directly enumerates files, reads content, checks existence, and constructs a live FileSystemWatcher in its constructor. Tests must depend on timing-sensitive real filesystem events, making missed-event, retry, overflow, and disposal scenarios difficult to reproduce reliably.
findings.recommendation: Separate synchronous scanning and document parsing from event monitoring, and inject small filesystem and watcher abstractions or factories. This permits deterministic tests for event ordering, failures, overflow recovery, and disposal without changing production behavior.
